An Indian NGO's donation website should publish a short, plain-language refund and cancellation policy and a terms page before it accepts a single rupee online, because donors, payment gateways and your own accounts team will all ask for them sooner or later. The refund policy states when a donation can be reversed (duplicate payments, wrong amounts, failed-but-debited transactions), how to ask, and how long you will take to answer; the cancellation section explains how a monthly donor stops a recurring gift; and the terms page sets out who you are, what the money is used for and what you do with donor data. This guide is for trustees and programme managers commissioning NGO website development in India who want these pages to be accurate, findable and usable rather than copied from an online-shop template.

It is written for registered trusts, societies and Section 8 companies that take donations through a website. It covers why these pages exist, what a donation refund policy should and should not promise, the cancellation rules for recurring gifts, the special cases (foreign contributions, restricted funds, tax receipts), where to place the links, how to word everything for a donor in a hurry, and what a developer needs to build around the pages. It does not give legal advice. Where a point depends on your registrations or on the rules of your payment provider, we say so and mark it for a lawyer or chartered accountant to confirm.

## Why a Donation Website Needs Refund and Terms Pages at All

There are three practical reasons, and none of them is that a law specifically demands a page with this exact title.

The first is your payment provider. When an NGO applies for a payment gateway or payment-link account, the provider's onboarding team usually reviews the website before approving the account. Reviewers commonly look for a contact page, a privacy policy, terms and a refund or cancellation policy, and applications are often sent back when one is missing. Requirements differ between providers and change over time, so read the current checklist of the provider you plan to use rather than relying on a blog, including this one. The pages are cheap to write and expensive to be rejected for.

The second is the donor. A person who has donated twice by mistake, or whose card was charged but who saw an error screen, wants to know within a minute whether that money is recoverable and whom to write to. If your site does not answer, they will ask their bank to reverse the charge, and a chargeback costs the organisation time and sometimes a fee on top of the lost gift. Our guide to the [donor help page for receipts, failed payments and corrections](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donor-help-page-receipts-failed-payments-corrections-2026) covers the support side; the policy pages are the written rules that support page points to.

The third is your own protection. A donor who later says "I thought this was refundable" is much easier to respond to when your checkout said, in plain words, what happens. Clear terms also help your team behave consistently: the person on the phone and the person replying to email give the same answer because the policy is written down.

### Donations are not shop purchases

Most refund policy templates found online are written for products: they talk about returns, restocking, delivery and 7-day windows. Copying one onto a donation page produces nonsense such as "items must be returned unused". A donation is a gift, normally made without receiving goods or services, and a well-drafted NGO policy says so. If you do sell anything through the same site, such as event tickets, merchandise or sponsored-meal packages with benefits, those need their own short terms, and the donation policy should not be stretched over them.

## What a Donation Refund Policy Should Say

Keep it to a page. Use headings so a donor can jump to the situation they are in. The sections below are a sensible structure; adapt the wording to your organisation and have it checked.

### 1. The general position

State the default honestly. Many organisations say that donations are voluntary gifts and are generally non-refundable once received, and then list the exceptions. This is clearer than hiding the position or promising refunds you do not intend to give. Whatever you decide, be consistent with what your checkout page and donation receipt say.

### 2. The exceptions you will honour

List the cases you will review, in concrete terms:

- **Duplicate payment.** The same donor paid the same amount twice within a short time because of a double click or a slow page.
- **Wrong amount.** The donor entered an amount with an extra zero or typed the wrong figure. Decide how long after the payment you will consider this, and say so.
- **Payment debited but donation not recorded.** The bank shows a debit but your system shows failure. In most cases the payment provider's own reconciliation either completes the payment or returns the money automatically, and the policy should tell the donor to wait for the stated period before writing to you. Do not give a number of days you cannot control; say "your bank or the payment provider will normally resolve this, and you can write to us if it has not been resolved after the period shown on your bank's or provider's page".
- **Unauthorised use of a card or UPI account.** Direct the donor to their bank first; offer your help in confirming whether a payment reached you.
- **Recurring payment taken after cancellation.** Covered in the next section.

### 3. How to ask

Give one email address and one form, and say what details to include: donor name, date, amount, payment reference or UTR, the phone number or email used and the reason. Avoid asking donors to send card numbers, and say so explicitly. A donation help page that asks for the donor's full card number in an email is a security incident waiting to happen.

### 4. What you will do and how long it takes

Commit to a reply window you can actually meet, such as acknowledging within a stated number of working days. Do not commit to the bank's processing time, which you do not control. A typical sentence is: "If we approve a refund, we will start it within X working days, and it will be returned to the original payment method. The time it takes to appear in your account depends on your bank." Fill in X with a number your accounts team has agreed to.

### 5. What happens to the tax receipt

If you have issued a tax-benefit receipt for a donation that is then refunded, the receipt must be cancelled or corrected. Say that you will cancel the receipt and, if applicable, issue a corrected one. Do not quote tax rules on this page; refer donors to their own advisers. [TODO for the NGO: confirm the wording with your chartered accountant, particularly if you hold approvals under the Income Tax Act.]

## Cancellation Rules for Recurring Donations

If your website offers monthly or annual giving, the cancellation terms matter more than the refund terms, because the complaint you will get most often is "I stopped, but you charged me again".

Our articles on [recurring monthly giving](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-recurring-monthly-giving-2026) and on the [RBI e-mandate rules for recurring donations](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-rbi-e-mandate-recurring-donations-2026) cover the technology and the payment rules. For the policy page, the points to put in writing are these:

1. **How the donor cancels.** Ideally the donor can cancel from a link in every receipt email or from a donor account page, without phoning anyone. If cancellation needs an email to the office, say so, and give the address.
2. **When cancellation takes effect.** State whether a cancellation made before a given cut-off prevents the next instalment. Because mandate processing happens through the donor's bank and the payment provider, there may be a lead time; ask your provider for the exact rule and write it down in your own words.
3. **Pausing and changing the amount.** Many donors do not want to stop; they want to give less for a few months. Offering "pause" and "change amount" in the same place reduces cancellations. Say whether you support them.
4. **Pre-debit notifications.** For card and UPI mandates, banks and providers send notices before a debit. Tell donors to expect them and not to ignore them, because a donor who ignores an alert and is surprised by a debit is the one who calls their bank.
5. **Failed instalments.** Explain what happens if an instalment fails: whether you retry, whether the donor is emailed and how many failures end the plan.

## Special Cases That Need Their Own Wording

### Foreign contributions

If your NGO is registered under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act and receives donations from abroad, the way those funds are handled is governed by FCRA rules, including the requirement that they go into a designated account. A refund of a foreign contribution is not just a customer-service decision. Do not promise automatic refunds on the general page; add one sentence saying that refunds of foreign contributions are handled case by case and in line with applicable rules, and then ask your FCRA compliance adviser how to deal with them. Our article on [FCRA payment gateway setup for NGOs](/blog/fcra-payment-gateway-setup-ngos) covers the account and gateway side.

### Restricted and campaign donations

If a donor gives to a specific campaign, such as a flood appeal, and you later receive more than you can use, what happens to the surplus is a policy question that donors do care about. Many organisations publish a short statement: funds given for a named campaign are used for it, and if the target is exceeded or the programme cannot go ahead, surplus funds are used for similar work, and donors are told. State what your trustees have actually decided. Do not copy another NGO's wording unless your board agrees with it. This is also covered, from the page-design side, in [fundraising progress bars and goal counters](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-fundraising-progress-bar-goal-thermometer-2026).

### Donations made on behalf of others

If a donation is made in someone's memory or as a gift, the person paying is the donor for the purposes of refunds and receipts. Say that refund requests are handled with the person who made the payment.

### Anonymous and cash-equivalent giving

Cheque, bank transfer and cash gifts are handled outside the gateway. If your terms page only talks about online donations, say so, so the policy does not accidentally promise refunds on offline gifts. See our guide to [offline donations, bank transfers, cheques and pledges](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-offline-donations-bank-transfer-cheque-cash-pledges-2026).

## The Terms Page: What to Include and What to Leave Out

A donation terms page is not a contract with pages of legal language. Its job is to tell a reasonable donor, in a few hundred words, the main conditions under which the site is used and gifts are accepted. A sensible outline:

- **Who we are.** Legal name, registration type and number, registered address and contact. Match what appears in the footer and on the [contact and grievance page](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-contact-grievance-page-trust-safeguarding-2026), because inconsistencies between pages are exactly what suspicious donors notice.
- **How donations are processed.** Name the payment provider or providers, and state that card and bank details are handled by them and not stored on your servers. Only say this if it is true for your build; ask your developer to confirm.
- **How donations are used.** A general statement of purpose and, if relevant, how unrestricted funds are allocated. Do not invent percentages. If you publish a breakdown, it should come from your audited accounts, with the year stated.
- **Receipts.** What receipt a donor receives, when, and how to correct details.
- **Privacy and data.** Link to the privacy policy; do not copy it. The data-protection side is covered in our article on [NGO donor data protection under the DPDP Act](/blog/ngo-donor-data-protection-dpdp-act-2026).
- **Website content.** A line that content on the site is for information, that images of beneficiaries are used with consent, and that you may update the site.
- **Governing law and contact for complaints.** A short statement that Indian law applies and where to send a grievance. Have a lawyer confirm the jurisdiction wording.

What to leave out: promises of tax savings (unless your accountant has cleared the exact sentence), guarantees about specific outcomes ("your gift will feed a child for a month" is an impact claim and needs evidence), and legal boilerplate you do not understand.

## Where to Put the Links

Pages that nobody can find do not protect anyone. Place links in four places:

1. **The donation form itself**, directly under the payment button, in small but legible text: "By donating you agree to our Terms and Refund Policy." Do not hide the line in light grey on white; it needs to pass a normal contrast check.
2. **The footer of every page**, together with the privacy policy, contact and grievance links.
3. **The receipt email**, so a donor looking for how to correct a payment finds the page from the message they already have.
4. **The donor help page**, as the written rules behind each answer.

A checkbox next to the button is sometimes added, and it can be sensible for recurring giving, where clear agreement to the mandate terms matters. For one-time gifts, an extra mandatory checkbox adds friction; discuss with your developer and, if possible, test both versions. Whatever you choose, your analytics should show whether the form's completion rate changes.

## Writing for a Donor in a Hurry

Policy pages fail when they read like a shop's legal notice. A few habits help:

- **Start with the answer.** "Most donations are final, but we will refund duplicates and mistakes. Here is how to ask." That sentence is more useful than three paragraphs of definitions.
- **Use the donor's words.** "Paid twice", "wrong amount", "stop my monthly gift" as headings, not "Chargeback Dispute Resolution".
- **Give a reading level a volunteer can follow.** If your donors read English as a second language, consider publishing a Hindi or Marathi version of the same page. Our article on [multilingual donation sites](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-multilingual-hindi-marathi-donation-site-2026) describes how to keep translated pages in step with the original.
- **Put a date on the page**, with "last updated" and a note of the main change. Old policies that contradict the checkout are a trust problem.
- **Be consistent.** Contradictions between the policy, the checkout page and the receipt are the usual cause of complaints.

## What the Developer Needs to Build Around the Pages

Publishing text is the easy part. The work for the development team is to make the process behind the words real.

- **A refund request form** that creates a ticket, with fields for payment reference, amount, date and reason, and an automatic acknowledgement to the donor. The form should not collect card numbers.
- **A donor-facing cancellation control** for recurring gifts, wired to the payment provider's cancel or pause function, with an email confirming the change.
- **Receipt cancellation and re-issue** inside your donor database, so that a refunded donation is marked as such and the receipt is not counted in reports or annual receipt summaries.
- **Reconciliation.** A daily comparison of provider settlement reports with your database, so that "debited but not recorded" cases are caught by you before the donor writes. See also our guide to [UPI donation reconciliation for NGOs](/blog/upi-donation-reconciliation-ngo-workflow).
- **An audit trail.** Who approved which refund, when and why. Auditors and trustees will ask.
- **Version history for the policy pages**, so you can show which text applied on a given date.

If your site runs on a donation platform you did not build, check whether it provides these functions before you write promises the system cannot keep. If you are planning a new build or a rebuild, include these items in the written brief; our [NGO website services](/pages/ngopage/) and [payment gateway integration](/services/payment-gateway) pages describe the kind of build we do.

## A Worked Example With Assumed Numbers

The numbers here are invented to show the process and are not benchmarks. Suppose an NGO receives one thousand online donations in a month and, after launching a clearer policy and a help page, finds that its team receives a small number of refund-related emails. Without a policy, the same team would have answered similar questions by phone and email in different ways, and some donors would have gone to their banks. The measurable gain is not a percentage we can promise; it is that each case now follows a written route: acknowledge, check the payment reference, check the provider's report, decide under the stated rules, cancel or re-issue the receipt, and record the decision.

To check whether this is working on your own site, track four things monthly: the number of refund and cancellation requests, the average time from request to reply, the number of requests that were "debited but not recorded", and the number of disputes raised through banks. If bank disputes rise while emails fall, donors are not finding the help page.

## Pre-Launch Checklist

1. A refund and cancellation policy exists, is in plain language and states a default position.
2. The exceptions listed match what your accounts team will really do.
3. The policy states how to ask, the details needed and the reply time you can meet.
4. Recurring-gift cancellation is described and works as described.
5. Foreign contribution handling is addressed, if you receive foreign funds.
6. The terms page names your legal entity, registrations and contact details exactly as in your footer.
7. The privacy policy is linked and matches how your forms handle data.
8. Links appear under the donation button, in the footer, in receipts and on the help page.
9. The receipts say how to correct details or request a cancellation.
10. A lawyer or chartered accountant has reviewed the final text. [TODO: record the reviewer and date internally.]
11. A test payment, refund request and recurring cancellation have been run end to end on the live site.
12. The pages carry a "last updated" date.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is an NGO required to have a refund policy on its donation website?
No single rule demands a page with that title, but payment providers commonly ask to see one when reviewing an NGO's website, and donors expect clear answers about mistaken or duplicate payments. Check the current onboarding checklist of your provider and take advice from a lawyer on your specific registrations.

### Can an NGO say that donations are non-refundable?
Many organisations state that donations are voluntary gifts and generally not refundable, while listing the cases they will review, such as duplicate or mistaken payments. That is more credible than a blanket promise or a hidden policy. Make sure your checkout page and receipts say the same thing.

### How should a monthly donor cancel a recurring donation?
Ideally from a link in the receipt email or from a donor account page, without needing to phone anyone. The policy should state how to cancel, when cancellation takes effect and what happens to a payment that is already being processed. Confirm the exact timing rules with your payment provider before writing them.

### What if a donor's money was debited but the donation was not recorded?
In many cases the payment provider's reconciliation either completes the payment or returns the money automatically. Tell donors how to check their bank or provider status, give them a way to send the payment reference to you, and run your own daily reconciliation so you find these cases first.

### Do we have to cancel the tax receipt if we refund a donation?
A receipt for a donation that is returned should be cancelled or corrected so that your records and the donor's claim are accurate. The correct procedure depends on your registrations, so ask your chartered accountant to confirm the wording and the steps.

## Where to Start

Write the one-paragraph default position first and agree it with your trustees; every other line follows from it. Then list the exceptions your team will honour, check each against your payment provider's rules, and only then ask a developer to build the form and the cancellation controls.
